questions.q: Per this lesson, what does a live whiteboard sketch reveal to a board that a prepared slide diagram does not?
options: Nothing -- both are evaluated identically
Only your artistic drawing ability, unrelated to architecture
How you think, since you're constructing the diagram in real time, often in response to an unanticipated question -- the board watches your sequencing, not just the final result
A live sketch is always strictly worse evidence of skill than a prepared diagram
questions.explain: A prepared diagram shows the design; a live sketch shows the thinking behind it, since the board watches it get built in real time and pays attention to sequencing as a signal of a sound mental model.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend deciding on a small, consistent visual vocabulary in advance rather than inventing diagram conventions on the spot?
options: Because review boards legally require a specific standard diagram notation
Because inventing conventions under pressure is a losing strategy, and consistency lets a board read the diagram far faster than if a different shape is used for each system with no reason
Because visual vocabulary has no effect on how quickly a board can follow a diagram
Because using varied shapes for similar things always demonstrates greater creativity and is preferred
questions.explain: Deciding on a small, practiced set of shapes and markings in advance avoids improvising under pressure, and consistent use (the same shape for every system, for example) lets the board read the diagram quickly rather than re-learning the notation each time it changes.

questions.q: What is the strongest live-whiteboarding technique this lesson describes for helping a board follow a diagram as it's built?
options: Drawing the entire diagram in silence and only explaining it once it's completely finished
Starting with the least important details first to save the best content for last
Building the diagram in a deliberate order, starting with the systems most central to the question, and narrating each addition as it's drawn
Avoiding narration entirely so the board can form their own interpretation
questions.explain: Building incrementally in a deliberate order and narrating each addition lets the board follow the reasoning as it's constructed live -- drawing in silence makes the board wait passively instead of following along.

questions.q: Which of these does this lesson identify as a live-whiteboarding execution mistake, independent of whether the underlying design is sound?
options: Using a consistent shape for every system drawn
Narrating each addition as it's drawn
Writing too small to be legible from where the board is sitting
Starting with the systems most central to the question being asked
questions.explain: Writing too small, drawing silently and narrating only at the end, running out of planned space, and excessive erasing/redrawing are all execution mistakes that cost points on legibility and pacing, separate from the design's actual quality -- the other three options are recommended practices, not mistakes.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the stronger way to handle running out of room mid-sketch for a component you still need to add?
options: Cram the new content into whatever space remains, regardless of legibility
Say out loud that you're restructuring for space, move to a clear area, and continue -- treating it as a normal part of live work rather than hiding it
Stop the whiteboarding exercise entirely and refuse to continue
Erase everything already drawn and start over without comment
questions.explain: Calmly announcing the need to restructure for space and continuing in a clear area is the recoverable, professional response -- boards have seen this happen to every candidate, and how it's handled visibly is itself part of what's evaluated, unlike silently cramming content into insufficient space.
